item.research_question: Does the nanolamellar morphology and chemical composition of a 3D-printed eutectic high-entropy alloy (EHEA) persist after a high-pressure BCC-to-FCC phase transition, and what is the mechanism behind the observed irreversibility?
item.material_system: Ni40Co20Fe10Cr10Al18W2 (3D-printed eutectic high-entropy alloy with nanolamellar BCC and FCC phases); FeCuNi ternary alloy (used for MD simulations)
item.processing_route: Additive manufacturing via laser-powder bed fusion (M290 EOS machine, 400 W ytterbium-fiber laser, 100 μm focal diameter) using gas-atomized powders (15–53 µm); static high-pressure compression in a diamond anvil cell to 30 GPa using a 4:1 methanol:ethanol pressure medium; MD simulations using an EAM potential for FeCuNi with pressure applied at 0.65 GPa/ps up to 130 GPa
item.test_conditions: High-pressure XRD in diamond anvil cell up to 30.6 GPa; high-resolution TEM/STEM imaging of pressure-recovered samples; MD simulations at 300 K with pressure ramping to 130 GPa and decompression to 0 GPa
key_findings: The BCC-to-FCC phase transition initiates at 9 GPa and completes to a single-phase FCC state at pressures above 9 GPa.
The nanolamellar morphology is retained after pressure cycling to 30.6 GPa, with both layers transforming to the FCC phase.
The chemical compositions of the dual-phase lamellae remain unchanged after pressure recovery, indicating a diffusionless transformation.
No specific orientation relationship exists between the pressure-induced FCC phase and the original FCC phase, suggesting homogeneous nucleation of multiple FCC variants.
The phase transformation is irreversible; the single-phase FCC structure is retained upon decompression to ambient pressure.
MD simulations show that the BCC-to-FCC transformation completes at 130 GPa, with the initial interphase boundary remaining stationary.
Residual compressive strain of 0.3% is observed in the decompressed FCC lattice compared to the ambient pressure FCC lattice.
item.mechanism: The authors propose that the irreversibility is driven by the disruption of the B2 ordered structure within the BCC phase during transformation, which makes the resulting FCC phase energetically more favorable. Additionally, the formation of a dislocation-less FCC phase with high morphological complexity (twin boundaries) creates a high energy barrier for the reverse FCC-to-BCC transition during decompression.
item.limitations: The authors state that due to limited choices of interatomic potentials, they could not find a suitable potential to simulate the phase transformation under high pressure for the specific EHEA Ni40Co20Fe10Cr10Al18W2, necessitating the use of a FeCuNi ternary alloy model for simulations.
item.future_work: The text does not explicitly state future work proposed by the authors.
quotes: Unlike traditional iron and steels, this alloy shows an irreversible BCC-to-FCC phase transformation under high pressures.
The chemical compositions of the dual-phase lamellae after pressure recovery remain unchanged, suggesting a diffusion-less BCC–FCC transformation in this EHEA.
The decreased stability of initial BCC phase can enhance the irreversibility.
